'''David Pines''' (June 8, 1924 {{ndash}} May 3, 2018) was a US physicist recognized for his work in quantum many-body systems in [[Condensed matter physics|condensed matter]] and [[nuclear physics]]. With his advisor [[David Bohm]], he contributed to the understanding of [[electron]] interactions in metals.<ref name=":0" /> Bohm and Pines introduced the [[plasmon]], the quantum of [[Plasma oscillation|electron density oscillations]] in metals.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Coleman |first1=Piers |last2=Greene |first2=Laura |date=2018-08-20 |title=David Pines (1924–2018) |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-018-05987-0 |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=560 |issue=7719 |pages=432 |doi=10.1038/d41586-018-05987-0|pmid=30127484 |bibcode=2018Natur.560..432C }}</ref> They pioneered the use of the [[random phase approximation]].<ref name=":0" /> His work with [[John Bardeen]], the [[Bardeen–Pines interaction]] between electrons and phonons led to the development of the [[BCS theory]] of [[superconductivity]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=David Pines :: Department of Physics and Astronomy - UC Davis |url=https://physics.ucdavis.edu/news-events/memorials/david-pines |access-date=2024-03-23 |website=physics.ucdavis.edu}}</ref><ref name=":1" /> Pines extended BCS theory to nuclear physics to explain [[Stable nuclide|stability]] of [[Isotope|isotopes]] with even and odd numbers of [[Nucleon|nucleons]].<ref name=":1" /> He also used the theory of [[superfluidity]] to explain the glitches in [[Neutron star|neutron stars]].<ref name=":1" /> 

Pines was a promoter of the concept of [[Emergence#In science|emergence in physics]].<ref name=":1" />

== Early life ==
David Pines was born to Sidney Pines, a mechanical engineer, and Edith Pines (née Adelman).<ref>https://www.wral.com/david-pines-93-insightful-and-influential-physicist-dies/17548826/?comment_order=forward, and Ancestry.com records</ref> He graduated from Highland Park High School in Dallas in 1940, and then studied at [[Black Mountain College]] for one year before enrolling at the [[University of California, Berkeley]]<ref name="uiuc_obit" />

Pines earned a bachelor's degree in physics from UC Berkeley in 1944, and began graduate work there. His studies were interrupted after his first semester when he was drafted into the navy. He served for two years, and then followed [[J. Robert Oppenheimer]], who had served as a mentor at Berkeley, to [[Princeton University]] in 1947. He earned his Ph.D. at Princeton under [[David Bohm]] in 1950.<ref name="coleman_obit" /><ref name="uiuc_obit" />

== Research and academic positions ==
Pines was the founding director of the [[Institute for Complex Adaptive Matter]] (ICAM) and the International Institute for Complex Adaptive Matter (I2CAM) (respectively, United States-wide and international institutions dedicated to research in and the understanding of emergent phenomena), distinguished [[professor]] of [[physics]], [[University of California, Davis]], research professor of physics and [[professor emeritus]] of physics and [[Electrical engineering|electrical]] and [[computer engineering]] in the Center for Advanced Study, [[University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign]] (UIUC), and a staff member in the office of the Materials, Physics, and Applications Division at the [[Los Alamos National Laboratory]].<ref name="uiuc_obit" />

He was the founding director of the Center for Advanced Study, UIUC (1968–70), was vice-president of the [[Aspen Center for Physics]] from 1968 to 1972, founder and  co-chair of  the US-[[USSR]] Cooperative Program in Physics, 1968–89; and a co-founder, vice-president,  chair of the board of trustees, and co-chair of the science board of the [[Santa Fe Institute]], from 1982 to 1996.

He was the organizer or co-organizer of fifteen workshops and two summer schools of theoretical physics, was an honorary trustee and honorary member of the [[Aspen Center for Physics]], and a member of the board of overseers at [[Sabancı University]] in [[Istanbul]].

== Late life ==
Pines died on May 3, 2018, due to [[pancreatic cancer]].<ref name="sante_fe_obit" />

==Research interests==
In 1956, Pines predicted the existence of electronic modes where electrons in different bands move coherently out of phase, which he dubbed "[[Pines' Demon|demon]]" modes, after [[James Clerk Maxwell]], since he thought he "lived too early to have a particle or excitation named in his honor."<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Pines |first1=David |title=Electron Interaction In Solids |journal=Canadian Journal of Physics |date=December 1956 |volume=34 |issue=12A |page=1392 |doi=10.1139/p56-154 |bibcode=1956CaJPh..34.1379P |url=https://cdnsciencepub.com/doi/10.1139/p56-154 |access-date=August 10, 2023 |ref=I have always thought it too bad that Maxwell lived too early to have a particle or excitation namecl in his honor. Therefore I suggest that in honor of Maxwell, and because we deal here with a case of distinct electron motion (or D.E.M.), we call these new excitations, "demons".|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Although Pines justified his etymological choice by making the term a half [[backronym]] (from D.E.M., which he claimed stood for "distinct electron motion"), the phenomenon is unrelated to Maxwell's [[Demon (thought experiment)|statistical mechanics demon]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Starr |first1=Michelle |title=For The First Time, Physicists Observe a 'Demon' Plasmon in an Exotic Material |url=https://www.sciencealert.com/physicists-have-observed-a-demon-plasmon-in-strontium-ruthenate |access-date=August 10, 2023 |publisher=Science Alert |date=August 10, 2023}}</ref> [[Pines' Demon|Pines' demon]] should not be confused with the more common acoustic plasmon which arise from low dimensionality in, for example, 2D- or quasi-2D-materials. In comparison, the demon arises only in multiband materials through opposing currents from different electronic bands, and is ''not'' tied to a particular dimensionality. His prediction of the demon was first observed experimentally in 2023 in [[Distrontium ruthenate|strontium ruthenate]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ali A. Husain, Edwin W. Huang, Matteo Mitrano, Melinda S. Rak, Samantha I. Rubeck, Xuefei Guo, Hongbin Yang, Chanchal Sow, Yoshiteru Maeno, Bruno Uchoa, Tai C. Chiang, Philip E. Batson, Philip W. Phillips & Peter Abbamonte |title=Pines' demon observed as a 3D acoustic plasmon in Sr2RuO4 |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |date=August 9, 2023 |volume=45 |issue=7977 |pages=66–70 |doi=10.1038/s41586-023-06318-8 |pmid=37558882 |pmc=10482684 |bibcode=2023Natur.621...66H |doi-access=free }}</ref>

His latest research topics concerned the search for the organizing principles responsible for emergent behavior in materials where unexpectedly new classes of behavior emerge in response to the strong and competing interactions among their elementary constituents. Some recent research results on correlated electron materials are the development of a consistent phenomenological description of protected magnetic behavior in the pseudogap state of underdoped cuprate superconductors and the discovery of the protected emergence of itinerancy in the Kondo lattice in heavy electron materials and its description using a two-fluid model. He remained interested in the superfluidity of neutron stars revealed by pulsar glitches and in elementary excitations in the helium liquids.<ref name="auto">{{cite web |last=Physics |first=Department of |title=David Pines - PHYSICS ILLINOIS |url=https://physics.illinois.edu/people/directory/profile/d-pines |website=physics.illinois.edu}}</ref>

== Awards and honors ==
His seminal contributions to the theory of many-body systems and to [[theoretical astrophysics]] were recognized by two [[Guggenheim Fellowship]]s,<ref name="auto" /> the [[Eugene Feenberg Memorial Medal|Feenberg Medal]], the Edward A. Frieman Prize for Excellence in Graduate Student Research, [[Dirac Medal and Lecture|Dirac]] and [[Drucker Medal|Drucker]] prizes, and by his election to the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]], [[American Philosophical Society]], [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]], [[Russian Academy of Sciences]], and [[Hungarian Academy of Sciences]] and visiting professorships at the [[California Institute of Technology]], College de France, [[Trinity College, Cambridge]], [[University of Leiden]], and the [[Université de Paris]].

David Pines was a member and fellow of:
* Member, [[National Academy of Sciences]]<ref name="auto"/>
* Member, [[American Philosophical Society]]<ref name="auto"/>
* Fellow, [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]]<ref name="auto"/>
* Foreign member, [[Russian Academy of Sciences]]<ref name="auto"/>
* Honorary member, [[Hungarian Academy of Sciences]]<ref name="auto"/>
* Fellow, [[American Association for the Advancement of Science|American Association for Advancement of Science]]<ref name="auto"/>
* Fellow, [[American Physical Society]]<ref name="auto"/>
* [[National Science Foundation]] Senior Postdoctoral Fellow in Copenhagen and Paris 1957–58
* [[Guggenheim Fellowship|John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Fellow]] 1962–63 and 1970–71
During his life he received many awards including:
* Lorentz Professor, [[Leiden University]] 1971
* [[Fritz London]] Memorial Lecturer ([[Duke University]]) 1972
* [[Giulio Racah]] Memorial Lecturer ([[Hebrew University of Jerusalem]]) 1974
* Marchon Lecturer ([[Newcastle University]]) 1976
* Sherman Fairchild Distinguished Scholar ([[California Institute of Technology|Caltech]]) 1977
* [[Eugene Feenberg]] Memorial Lecturer ([[Washington University in St. Louis]]) 1982
* Eastman Kodak - [[University of Rochester]] Distinguished Lecturer 1983
* Friemann Prize in Condensed Matter Physics 1983
* [[Dirac Medal (UNSW)|Dirac Medal]] for the Advancement of Theoretical Physics ([[University of New South Wales]]) 1985
* Emil Warburg Lecturer ([[University of Bayreuth]]) 1985
*[[Eugene Feenberg Memorial Medal|Eugene Feenberg Medal]] 1985
* Daniel C. Drucker Eminent Faculty Award 1994
* {{ill|John Bardeen Prize|de}} for Superconductivity Theory 2009<ref name="aps.org">{{cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Pines&first_nm=David&year=2016|title=Sylvester James Gates, Jr.|website=www.aps.org}}</ref>
* [[Lilienfeld Prize|Julius Edgar Lilienfeld Prize]] 2016 <ref name="aps.org"/>
